p: There is no situation for a city in all the world to equal that of Constantinople. It stands upon a triangle of hills between two seas, the Black Sea to the north and the Sea of Marmara to the south, joined by the narrow strait of the Bosphorus; it commands the crossing from Europe into Asia; and beside it lies a deep and sheltered harbour, the Golden Horn, so called, some say, from the wealth that flowed into it. Whoever holds it holds the gate of two continents and the key of two seas. It is no wonder that it was, for fifteen centuries, the city that every conqueror desired.

There had been a Greek town there for a thousand years, called Byzantium, founded according to tradition by colonists from Megara, whose leader was named Byzas. In the year three hundred and twenty-four, the emperor Constantine, having become sole ruler of the Roman world, chose the site for a new capital, and on the eleventh of May, three hundred and thirty, he dedicated it as New Rome. Men soon called it the city of Constantine, Constantinople. He adorned it with statues and treasures stripped from the cities of the empire, gave it a senate, and fed its people free bread like the people of old Rome. It was from the beginning a Christian city, with churches where Rome had temples, though Constantine was not above setting up a great statue of himself as the sun god on a column in his forum.

When the western empire fell in the fifth century, the eastern empire, ruled from Constantinople, survived. Its people called themselves Romans to the very end, and so they were, in law, in government and in their own minds. We call their state the Byzantine Empire, after the old name of the city, a term invented by scholars long afterwards and one which its people would not have recognised. They spoke Greek, they were Christians of the Orthodox church, and they were Romans. It is a combination that historians of the West, brought up to think that the Roman Empire ended in four hundred and seventy-six, have never quite known what to do with.

The greatest of the emperors of New Rome was Justinian, who reigned from five hundred and twenty-seven to five hundred and sixty-five. His generals reconquered Africa from the Vandals and Italy from the Goths, for a time; his lawyers gathered the whole vast body of Roman law into a single code, which, rediscovered in Italy six hundred years later, became the foundation of the law of most of continental Europe; and his architects built the church of Hagia Sophia, meaning Holy Wisdom, whose immense dome seems, in the words of a writer who saw it built, not to rest upon solid masonry but to be suspended from heaven by a golden chain. When it was finished, Justinian is said to have exclaimed that he had surpassed Solomon. For nearly a thousand years it was the largest church in Christendom. His wife, the empress Theodora, had been an actress, a profession of the lowest repute, and was, by the malicious account of the historian Procopius, a woman of scandalous life; she was also, by every account, a woman of great courage, who, when a riot in the city threatened to drive her husband from his throne, refused to flee, saying that royalty is a good burial shroud. The riot was put down, with the slaughter of thirty thousand people in the Hippodrome.

For eight hundred years, Constantinople stood between Europe and the successive powers of the East. It was besieged by Persians and Avars together in six hundred and twenty-six, and by the Arabs, in the first flush of the expansion of Islam, in six hundred and seventy-four to six hundred and seventy-eight, and again in seven hundred and seventeen. It survived each time, defended by its great triple walls on the land side, built under the emperor Theodosius the Second, and by a secret weapon, the so-called Greek fire, a liquid that burned even on water and was sprayed from tubes on the prows of the emperors' ships. Its composition was so closely guarded that it is unknown to this day. Had the city fallen to the Arabs in the seventh or eighth century, the history of Europe might have been very different. Some historians have said so; others think the danger exaggerated. I incline to the former.

The city was also a treasure-house of learning. Its scholars preserved and copied the works of the ancient Greeks, Plato, Aristotle, Homer, the dramatists and the mathematicians, when they were all but forgotten in the West. A great part of what we possess of ancient Greek literature has come to us through Byzantine manuscripts.

Its fall, when it came, was the work of Christians first. In twelve hundred and four, the knights of the Fourth Crusade, who had set out to recover Jerusalem from the Muslims, were diverted, by the debts they owed to Venice and the intrigues of a Byzantine pretender, to Constantinople, which they stormed and sacked with a savagery that the Greek church has never forgotten. They stripped the churches, melted down statues of the ancient masters for their bronze, and set a prostitute on the throne of the patriarch in Hagia Sophia. The four bronze horses that stand above the doorway of Saint Mark's in Venice were part of the loot. The Byzantines recovered their city in twelve sixty-one, but the empire never recovered its strength.

The end came on the twenty-ninth of May, fourteen hundred and fifty-three, when the young Ottoman sultan Mehmed the Second, after a siege of some seven weeks, in which his engineers used enormous cannon to batter the ancient walls, took the city by storm. The last emperor, Constantine the Eleventh, died fighting in the breach, and his body was never certainly found. Mehmed rode to Hagia Sophia and turned it into a mosque. Constantinople became the capital of the Ottoman Empire, which in my own day still rules it, though the newspapers speak of that empire as the sick man of Europe. The Encyclopaedia informs me that the sick man will die in the next century, and that the city, under the new Turkish republic that succeeds him, will take the name by which its people had long called it, Istanbul, a name that comes, it is said, from a Greek phrase meaning into the city. It is a fitting name. For fifteen centuries, everyone was trying to get into it.
